The HALEU bottleneck moves downstream

The visible constraint on advanced reactors is HALEU supply. The United States still lacks a mature commercial supply chain for uranium enriched above 5% and below 20% U-235. Enrichment, deconversion, fuel fabrication and reactor construction remain large, obvious schedule risks.

By Bottleneck Briefs · Published 2026-07-03 · 14 min read

In brief

  • 1,271 kg | DN30-20’s maximum certified HALEU UF6 payload
  • 40–50 cylinders | Urenco’s 2026–2027 exemption campaign
  • Four packages | Project Pele’s initial HALEU TRISO fuel delivery
  • 2027–2028 | likely transition window from workarounds to standing package routes

The bottleneck moves with the fuel

Photo

NAC OPTIMUS-L canisters/fabrication

DOE used this image in its HALEU transport explainer that says optimized packages are needed to avoid excessive shipment counts.

Open source visual from DOE Office of Nuclear Energy

Reuse: license unclear - rights not verified · Attribution: Courtesy of NAC International via DOE

Transport becomes important later. A developer encounters the package constraint after obtaining material, selecting a fuel form and preparing a licensed facility to receive it. At that point, the question changes from whether HALEU exists to whether a specific material can move through a specific certified configuration at a commercially tolerable payload.

This is a sequential gate rather than a universal bottleneck. It binds when upstream work has progressed faster than the combination of Part 71 authority, criticality-validation evidence, package manufacturing, facility procedures and available package serials.

That distinction matters because a certificate is not a general passport for enriched uranium. Its authorization covers defined contents, enrichments, geometries, masses, absorbers and operating conditions. A configuration approved for TRISO compacts does not automatically cover UF6, metallic fuel, oxide powder, pebbles or fissile salts.

The most defensible conclusion is therefore narrower than “transport is the next major HALEU shortage.” Transport is an intermittently binding handoff constraint whose importance varies by campaign and fuel form.

Certification is only one part of shipment readiness

The operating asset is not a steel container. It is a complete shipment system:

approved content → validated analysis → certified package → manufactured package or cylinder → registered user → qualified procedures → carrier and route → authorized receiving facility

Each link can lag the others.

HALEU creates a more demanding criticality problem than conventional commercial UF6 transport below 5% enrichment. Package analyses must address moderation, water intrusion, damaged geometry, neutron absorbers, package arrays and hypothetical accident conditions. The applicable evidence base must also be strong enough to quantify analytical bias and uncertainty.

Orano’s DN30-X illustrates the engineering trade-off. The design combines the existing DN30 protective package with a new 30B-X cylinder containing boron-bearing criticality controls. The DN30-10 configuration permits up to 1,460 kilograms of UF6 at enrichment up to 10%. DN30-20 permits 1,271 kilograms at up to 20%.

A conventional 30B cylinder is associated with a 2,277-kilogram UF6 reference capacity. The optimized HALEU configurations therefore achieve certification by adding criticality controls and accepting lower payloads.

The certificate solved the analytical design problem, but it did not immediately create a generally available operating fleet. Orano began serial production of ten 30B-10 cylinders in May 2025. One year later, NRC records showed that manufacturing, standards incorporation and Urenco USA’s facility implementation were still not ready for Urenco’s contracted shipment need.

That gap between approval and operational availability is the central commercialization issue. (NRC Urenco exemption)

The named cases show an uneven market

The evidence does not describe one national transport shortage. It describes several fuel-form-specific markets at different stages of maturity.

The records are drawn from NRC, DOE, INL, Orano and NAC disclosures, including the Project Pele delivery record.

Project Pele is the clearest evidence that the transport gate can already be solved. INL received the microreactor’s HALEU TRISO fuel in late 2025. NAC reported that four OPTIMUS-L systems carried the initial core in one legal-weight truck shipment.

That shipment establishes much more than package certification. It demonstrates content qualification, physical hardware, package preparation, loading, transportation, receiving-site integration and field execution for one bounded TRISO campaign.

Urenco shows the opposite configuration. The company had higher-enrichment UF6 contracts and a licensed enrichment facility, but the optimized DN30-X and 30B-10 route was not ready for its schedule. NRC therefore authorized a narrow exemption using the existing DN30 and standard 30B architecture.

The exemption permits approximately 40–50 cylinders during 2026–2027 for one customer, within the 5–10% enrichment band. It is a functional bridge, but not a scalable general regime. It depends on a restricted content envelope, defined shipment count, specific safety analysis and no physical package redesign.

These two cases should be read together. Project Pele proves that HALEU transport is feasible and operational for an approved TRISO configuration. Urenco proves that a certificate-and-fleet mismatch can still appear when a different fuel form reaches the shipment interface.

The evidence bottleneck sits beneath the hardware

The hardest constraint may not be package fabrication. It may be the evidence required to justify the package’s content and payload.

The 2024 DNCSH presentation described a benchmark inventory containing more than 5,000 criticality benchmarks and approximately 430 HALEU experiments. Only about 19 were considered relevant to non-light-water-reactor HALEU configurations, and 11 of those predated 1980.

Those counts are approximate and dated, but the shape of the problem is clear. A large nominal database does not necessarily contain experiments applicable to a specific fuel form, geometry, moderator, absorber or enrichment range.

DOE and the national laboratories are addressing this through the Criticality Safety for Commercial-Scale HALEU initiative. The program covers UF6 cylinders, TRISO pebbles and compacts, enrichment ranges between established experimental regimes, chlorine-bearing systems, moderator effects and safety-important materials.

The THETA project is one example. Led through the national-laboratory system with Kairos Power participation, it examines water infiltration and neutron behavior in TRISO pebble transport configurations. DOE reported that the initial experimental campaign had been completed by April 2025.

Another project revisits historical Y-12 and Oak Ridge Critical Experiments Facility work involving enriched UF6 cylinders. The reason is unusually concrete: the relevant historical experiments had not been incorporated into the international benchmark handbook for the intended application.

A TerraPower-related effort addresses chlorine configurations for molten-chloride fuel-cycle operations. It demonstrates why HALEU transport cannot become one standardized market. The evidence needed for UF6 bears little resemblance to the evidence required for TRISO pebbles or fissile chloride salts.

The closest historical analogue is the expansion of fresh light-water-reactor fuel transport above the traditional 5% enrichment range. That earlier transition was resolved through additional experiments, validated analyses and package approvals.

The same mechanism is operating now, but the present problem is more fragmented. Advanced reactors use a wider range of fuel forms, enrichments, geometries and process routes. Standardization may therefore occur through several package families rather than one dominant design.

Commercialization is now a service problem

The market has moved beyond pure technical feasibility. The unresolved question is whether package access can be procured repeatedly.

A functioning commercial service requires available package serials, cylinders, maintenance capacity, inspection equipment, approved quality-assurance programs, trained operators, controlled procedures, carrier availability and receiving-site compatibility. It also requires scheduling across enrichment, deconversion and fabrication facilities that may themselves be operating near first-of-a-kind conditions.

Orano’s fleet-sharing model shows one possible commercial structure. Rather than requiring each customer to own a dedicated fleet, the provider pools packages and supplies storage, inspection, maintenance, recertification, tracking and availability management.

This changes the customer’s expenditure from package ownership toward reserved access and recurring services. It also transfers idle-capacity, maintenance and availability risk to the fleet operator.

NAC’s Project Pele work shows a more integrated alternative. The package holder can combine licensing, hardware preparation, field operators, shipment planning and execution. In that model, control lies not only in the certificate but in the ability to deliver an end-to-end regulated movement.

DOE’s $11 million package program is best understood as capability formation, not evidence of a large existing transport market. The five recipients—NAC International, Westinghouse, Container Technologies Industries, American Centrifuge Operating and Paragon D&E—are working on modifications or new concepts with maximum development periods of two or three years.

The likely regulatory conversion window is therefore 2027–2028. Modifications to existing packages should generally reach filing before clean-sheet designs because they inherit an established package architecture, operating basis and analysis history.

The stronger commercialization test is not whether a recipient files an application. It is whether a named customer subsequently procures a package, registers as a user and completes repeated shipments under normal certificate conditions.

Value will migrate toward control of the interface

The certificate holder controls the design basis and modification history. The user controls loading, handling, shipment, storage and maintenance under an approved quality-assurance program. National laboratories and NRC influence the validation methods and evidence considered acceptable. Fuel-cycle companies control the timing and form of demand.

This creates several potential revenue layers:

  • package and cylinder manufacturing;
  • certificate applications and content amendments;
  • package leasing and fleet reservations;
  • inspection, maintenance, repair and recertification;
  • shipment planning, loading and field services;
  • quality assurance, document control and configuration management.

The recurring economic position may be more attractive than one-time fabrication. A company that combines certificate continuity, available fleet capacity, maintenance records, approved procedures and customer integration can become difficult to replace even when the underlying metal package is reproducible.

The evidence does not yet show that these positions earn high margins. Public records do not disclose package selling prices, lease rates, fleet utilization, availability guarantees, delay penalties, warranties, insurance costs or customer concentration.

The distinction between new value and transferred value is also important. Moving from customer-owned packages to pooled leasing may shift revenue to a fleet provider without increasing total system expenditure. A higher-capacity package may generate more package rent while reducing carrier trips, labor, security and handling costs.

Public-company exposure is similarly indirect. Centrus Energy participates through HALEU enrichment and American Centrifuge Operating’s package-development award. BWX Technologies and GE Vernova appear in adjacent deconversion and fuel-cycle programs. Cameco has an indirect connection through its ownership interest in Westinghouse. Kanadevia owns NAC International.

None is a pure transport-package exposure, and transport economics may remain immaterial relative to the companies’ larger businesses. The relevant analytical question is not which listed company “wins,” but which entity controls an interface that customers cannot readily bypass.

The strongest counterargument is already visible

The package thesis can be overstated in four ways.

First, upstream constraints remain larger. Centrus produced 900 kilograms of HALEU by June 2025, and DOE contracted for an additional 900 kilograms. That is meaningful progress, but small relative to the quantities required for a mature reactor fleet.

DOE’s broader enrichment awards also show where public money is concentrated. Of the $2.7 billion in task orders announced in January 2026, $1.8 billion was explicitly directed to HALEU capacity through American Centrifuge Operating and General Matter. Orano’s $900 million task order covered LEU rather than HALEU.

Second, fabrication can bind before transport. NRC issued TRISO-X’s Category II fuel-fabrication license in February 2026, nearly four years after the initial application. Yet TX-1 remained under construction and still required startup-readiness inspection before receiving special nuclear material and operating commercially.

Third, exemptions may remain an adequate bridge while shipment volumes are low. Urenco’s case shows that NRC can authorize a constrained legacy route without waiting for an optimized system. Repeated exemptions could reduce customers’ willingness to pay for scarce optimized-package access.

Fourth, technical relief may arrive before durable pricing power develops. Existing package families, public benchmark programs, DOE-funded designs and incumbent modifications may create overlapping capacity by the late 2020s. Package access could become routine just as upstream HALEU volume becomes large enough to support it.

The strongest falsifier would be multiple unaffiliated users completing recurring commercial-quantity campaigns under standing certificates, with ordinary lead times and no urgent amendments, exemptions or fleet-slot problems. At that point, transport would have become a specialized operating cost rather than a deployment gate.

What to watch

  • By December 2027, a completed U.S. 30B-10 shipment under CoC 9388 without Urenco’s exemption.
  • By December 2028, an NRC Part 71 filing tied to a 2025 DOE package-award recipient.
  • By December 2029, a DNCSH or post-2024 benchmark cited in a package review.
  • Additional Urenco-style exemptions for HALEU shipments after upstream material is contractually available.
  • By December 2030, two unaffiliated users completing at least two non-exempt campaigns each.

The practical conclusion

HALEU transport is neither a solved commodity service nor the dominant constraint across advanced reactors. It is an uneven interface in early deployment.

One TRISO campaign has crossed the gate. A commercial-quantity UF6 campaign has required a regulatory workaround. Certified packages exist, but package availability, standards incorporation, facility procedures and content-specific evidence remain uneven.

Through roughly 2027–2028, this interface is likely to bind intermittently when individual campaigns progress faster than package implementation. Beyond that window, the question shifts from technical availability to procurement quality: fleet depth, lead times, recurring users, maintenance capacity and standing regulatory authority.

The strategic control point is not uranium ownership alone. It is the ability to convert qualified HALEU into a repeatable, regulator-approved shipment without forcing the customer to rebuild the logistics chain for every campaign.
